falter

/FAWL-tur/ — rhymes with alter · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To falter is to lose strength or confidence and begin to waver.

Her voice faltered when she reached the sad part of the speech.

Worked Example

The sprinter, leading the race with fifty meters to go, suddenly faltered as self-doubt crept in, and his pace slowed dramatically.

Falter captures both the physical slowing and the mental loss of confidence — it's not just 'slowed down,' it's the moment when nerve breaks. That combination of weakness and hesitation is what makes falter more precise than 'slowed.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

hesitate: To hesitate is to pause because you are unsure whether to continue — a purely mental stall, with your strength untouched. To falter is bigger: confidence and strength give way together, so the pause comes with real weakening. A speaker hesitates over one word; a speaker falters mid-speech.

weaken: To weaken is simply to lose strength or force — a battery weakens, a signal weakens — with no suggestion of doubt attached. Falter adds the human wobble: when a runner falters, the failing strength arrives braided with hesitation and slipping nerve. Weaken is physical; falter is body and nerve at once.

yield: To yield is to give way under pressure — the struggle ends and the other side wins. To falter is to waver while still fighting: strength and confidence slip, but nothing has been surrendered yet. Faltering is the wobble along the way; yielding is the moment resistance stops.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

persist: to keep going despite difficulty

rally: to regain strength and press on

Where it sits · how completely strength gives way — stumble → falter → crumble → collapse

stumble vs. falter: Stumble is lighter than falter — a runner who stumbles trips once and recovers, while one who falters is losing strength or confidence step by step.

crumble vs. falter: Crumble is stronger than falter: when courage falters it wavers and hesitates, but when it crumbles it is actively breaking apart.

collapse vs. falter: Collapse is the extreme far beyond falter — a faltering effort loses strength and confidence and begins to waver, while a collapsing one gives way completely all at once.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — falter

Root — falter: to stagger, hesitate (Middle English (ultimate origin uncertain))

Put it together

Put it together: Falter arrived in Middle English meaning 'to stagger or totter' — the picture of unsteady legs carried over to any strength, voice, or confidence that wobbles and begins to give way.

Use the root in a new word: faltering

Use the root in a new word: faltering: The team made a faltering start to the season, hesitating and losing ground in game after game — faltering is simply falter in action.

Word Building

Word Choice

neutral / formal

Falter describes the moment when both confidence and ability fail together — that critical breakdown when nerve breaks. In everyday conversation, 'hesitate' or 'slow down' might be clearer, but falter paints a vivid picture of that internal collapse.
